Our key insight is that the effect of each transformation can be approximated as a perturbation to the model weights, allowing us to jointly train the model with a benign loss on the original model and a malicious loss on each simulated transformed model. These perturbations are simple enough to simulate at every training iteration across diverse transformations, making them practically combinable within a single training objective, enabling a unified attack. Through extensive experiments across attack scenarios, model families, and a wide range of deployment-time model transformations, we show that our attack achieves high success rates. This demonstrates that model transformations may be utilized to trigger significantly different behavior from the original model and reinforces the associated security concerns by demonstrating that a single attack can jointly target diverse transformations.

papers.title: Individual Fairness via Local Predictive Consistency
papers.summary: Individual fairness in machine learning requires that similar individuals receive similar predictions. Most existing definitions are pairwise in nature, imposing a Lipschitz constraint that must hold either globally across all pairs of data instances or locally within specified neighborhoods. In practice, however, such pairwise constraints may be overly restrictive and may not directly identify which individuals receive locally inconsistent predictions. We study local predictive consistency as a node-level relaxation of pairwise individual fairness, where each prediction is compared with a similarity-weighted average of predictions in its local neighborhood. This yields an interpretable node-level fairness score and a corresponding regularized learning approach based on local residuals. Since graph-based individual fairness depends critically on the underlying similarity structure, we make the construction of the neighborhood graph explicit and discuss threshold selection through graph-coverage diagnostics. Our approach applies to binary classification, regression, and time-to-event prediction. We further compare this formulation with pairwise constraint-based approaches and analyze the resulting fairness--performance trade-offs.

papers.title: A Causal Bootstrap for Diverse Image Generation under Unobserved Confounding

papers.title: Regularity-Aware Stochastic MGDA with Adaptive Per-Iterate Conflict-Avoidant Update

Furthermore, to reduce value-learning cost, the critic retains only early Transformer blocks from the pretrained checkpoint used to initialize the actor. Critic-depth comparisons further show strong task performance with substantially lower critic-side computation. These results demonstrate that coordinating turn- and token-level credit with a lightweight shared critic improves agent performance while keeping value estimation efficient. papers.title: Privacy Accounting for Empirical Denoisers
papers.summary: Diffusion models have emerged as the foundation of modern generative systems, yet their high memorization capacity raises privacy concerns. While differentially private (DP) training provides formal guarantees, it comes at a cost in sample quality. In this work, we study a complementary question: how much privacy loss is incurred during the sampling process itself? Directly analyzing modern neural denoisers is challenging because their sensitivity to a single training example is generally intractable. To overcome this challenge, we construct and analyze a clipped privacy-accountable empirical denoiser, a training-free estimator of the Bayes-optimal denoiser, whose per-step sensitivity can be computed explicitly, allowing each denoising step to be a Gaussian mechanism. This perspective enables privacy accounting under Gaussian DP when each training example contributes to each denoising step, and under $f$-DP trade-off functions when each generated sample uses a single randomly subsampled block of the training data. We report every $(\varepsilon, δ)$ guarantee as a certified upper bound from a privacy loss distribution accountant, and use a cumulant-based Edgeworth approximation as a fast diagnostic, characterizing where it is reliable and where it becomes anti-conservative. We also analyze the privacy loss along the denoising trajectory and show that it grows steeply near the critical window in which semantic content is formed. This observation motivates hybrid samplers that use the private empirical denoiser through the formative steps where it remains a faithful proxy for the neural denoiser, then switch to a public neural denoiser for the remaining refinement. Our results on CIFAR-10 and CelebA-64 show that the privacy of diffusion models depends not only on the training procedure, but also on sampling-time design choices such as subsampling, stopping time, and hybrid denoising.

papers.title: Learning Positive Linear Combinations of ReLUs in Fully Polynomial Time

On a technical level, our approach develops a novel boosting procedure of a ``weak'' learner that recovers the hidden weight vectors to constant error, in a list-decodable manner. To develop this ``weak'' learning procedure, we leverage implicit tensor computation techniques to construct a low-degree filtering procedure based on Hermite tensors of the target function. This procedure amplifies separation among (clusters of) weight vectors to learn each of them to constant error. We then argue that the same procedure can be used for improving the estimation of hidden weight vectors, using gradient descent-like updates on the Euclidean sphere. A crucial ingredient of our algorithm is a pruning approach that ensures only relevant vectors that approximate the hidden weight vectors at target accuracy are maintained by the algorithm.

papers.title: Maximum Likelihood on the Joint (Data, Condition) Distribution for Solving Ill-Posed Problems with Conditional Flow Models
papers.summary: In the absence of conditioning information, normalizing flow models are trained using maximum likelihood. papers.title: Adaptive Frequency Threshold Byte Pair Encoding for Mixed Natural Language and Structured Symbolic Corpora

papers.title: Neural-DISCO: Source-Conditioned Counterfactual Editing of Neural Population Activity
papers.summary: Understanding how neural activity encodes behavioral and sensory variables is a key challenge in systems neuroscience. This requires models that go beyond predicting activity from labels and instead support source-conditioned counterfactual editing: given a recorded source response, we should be able to edit one measured behavioral or stimulus label and predict how neural activity would change while preserving other observed labels and source-specific variability not explained by the labels. Neural-DISCO partitions the latent space into label-specific components, each associated with an observed behavioral or stimulus label, together with a residual latent that captures variability not supplied through observed labels. Across simulated and real neural recording datasets, we show that this structure enables selective editing of measured labels to generate counterfactual neural responses while preserving the remaining content of the original activity. Further, to gain insight into how behavioral and stimulus labels are encoded at single-neuron resolution, we pair this disentangled framework with feature attribution methods that identify which neurons are most important for each label. We find that disentanglement enhances the recovery of known functional cell roles in both synthetic and real data. Together, these results support Neural-DISCO as a framework for counterfactual modeling of neural activity and provide a practical interface for probing how neural populations encode behavior and sensory information. papers.title: Trusting the Tool: Asymmetric Deference of LLM Vulnerability Auditors to Static-Analysis Evidence
papers.summary: Pipelines that combine large language models (LLMs) with static analysis let the model consume the analyser's output as evidence, but whether the model distinguishes true from false evidence, and whether its scrutiny depends on what the evidence claims, has not been measured. False evidence acted asymmetrically: relative to true notes about the same operations, false assurances lowered the detection of real vulnerabilities by up to 19 points, whereas false alarms never significantly lowered accuracy and were disputed far more often. An internally registered replication on seven new models confirmed that false assurances move verdicts towards their claim more than false alarms do (mean asymmetry +0.16, 95% CI +0.10 to +0.24). Instructions in the audit prompt did not reliably reduce deference; the best one failed to replicate. Verifying each claim in a separate call and showing the refuted claims raised accuracy under false assurances by 12 points in a pre-specified test (p=0.002) without loss under true evidence; for a second model the gain was smaller and not significant. Pipelines should therefore verify a tool's guarantees before the model relies on them, and studies should measure deference in a direction-aware way.

papers.title: Residual-Based Adaptive Refinement in Hybrid Variational-Collocation PINNs for Singular Elliptic PDEs with Mixed Dirichlet-Neumann Boundary Conditions
papers.summary: Solutions of second-order elliptic PDE problems on nonconvex or cracked domains with mixed Dirichlet-Neumann conditions typically lie outside $H^2(Ω)$. The loss combines a variational residual tested against Legendre bubble functions, a strong-form collocation term and penalties for the Dirichlet and Neumann data. The method is tested on five two dimensional benchmarks, namely a Mode~III crack, a cross-shaped domain with four re-entrant corners with unequal amplitude, a reaction-diffusion problem with four localized peaks, a monotone semilinear problem with a boundary layer and the Motz problem. papers.title: Singular Geometry of Low-Rank Adaptation
papers.summary: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) is now a standard approach to parameter-efficient fine-tuning of large neural networks. Its low-rank factorization is inherently non-identifiable, making LoRA a singular statistical model whose learning complexity cannot be described by parameter dimension alone. We study this complexity using the real log canonical threshold (RLCT) from singular learning theory and how it depends on both the low-rank parameterization and the pretrained network. Under a local linearization, LoRA induces a low-rank trace regression model whose Kullback--Leibler geometry is controlled by a forward-backward covariance, constructed from activations and backpropagated sensitivities at the adapted layer. This covariance determines which low-rank perturbations are statistically observable. When it is nondegenerate along the relevant low-rank directions, we recover the classical learning complexity of reduced-rank regression; when its kernel meets these directions, additional statistically indistinguishable parameters change the singular geometry. We characterize this geometry locally through observable tangent directions and a residual singularity, and globally through affine linear sections of determinantal varieties. The global learning complexity need not be determined at a ground-truth parameter, as singularities on another rank stratum can dominate. We also introduce a curvature-corrected multi-temperature estimator of the RLCT. Experiments on multilayer perceptron and transformer architectures reveal strongly layer-dependent forward-backward geometry and show that ambient covariance degeneracy does not imply degeneracy along the low-rank directions relevant to adaptation.

papers.title: Neural LoFi with Backward Coupling: A Spectral Theory of Cross-Layer Feature Learning

papers.title: Generalization properties of the token perceptron: the role of embedding and vocabulary
papers.summary: Large language models are trained to predict tokens from a finite vocabulary, each represented by a vector in a $d$-dimensional embedding space. We call this the \textit{token perceptron}. We compute its generalization error with the replica method, taking $N\to\infty$ at fixed number of examples per position $α=P/N$ and keeping $d$ and the vocabulary size $D$ finite. As a first reference case, we consider continuous embeddings on the sphere, which isolate the role of the embedding dimension. The natural load is then $α/d$, and for $d>1$ a normalized label fixes the direction of the teacher output, so the problem becomes a noiseless regression: the teacher is recovered exactly above $α_{\rm rec}=d^2/(d-1)$, and spherical cross-entropy reaches this threshold at large inverse temperature. In the same setting the storage capacity of random associations scales as $d^2$ for margins $O(1/\sqrt{d})$. We then turn to vocabulary embeddings, where a label only identifies the Voronoi cell of the teacher output, so that each example imposes inequalities rather than equations, as in the classical perceptron. We compute the Bayes-optimal error for a given embedding matrix through an approximate spectral closure and show that the optimal learner first resolves the directions in which the vocabulary has the largest variance, even when the teacher is isotropic.

papers.title: Isotropic Activation Functions Enable Deindividuated Neurons and Adaptive Topologies
papers.summary: Varying the number of neurons while preserving function is difficult because neural networks' dense connectivity creates strong computational interdependence between units. These symmetry-led diagonalisation and structural changes prioritise function-invariance: neurogenesis exactly preserves function, neurodegeneration is asymptotically function-preserving with the pruned singular-value threshold. Moreover, this construction enables asymptotic 50\% parameter sparsification of dense networks while preserving function analytically. Thus, the approach enables real-time restructuring of the architecture in response to task demands, task appending, removal or changes. Conceptually, this motivates broader applications of symmetry prescriptions at the small scale, even when no data-driven model-scale symmetry adherence is required. Following this, we build activations around symmetry, not from classical assumptions about individual neurons. Unlike typical elementwise forms, these alternatives feature explicit basis independence and do not individuate neurons. We leverage this to decompose and reinterpret neurons across sequential layers, simplifying structure and providing a natural route to adaptive topologies. papers.summary: Data stream classification under concept drift and class imbalance requires models to adapt continuously while maintaining strong minority-class performance. Many existing approaches rely on active memory management, in- cluding instance removal, memory restructuring, resampling, and synthetic data generation. PAI-KNN main- tains a simple sliding-window buffer and dynamically adjusts its decision rule using class prior estimates derived from recent observations. Evaluated on a mul- titude of synthetic data streams covering various imbalance and drift scenarios, PAI-KNN achieves competitive performance with state-of-the-art methods, per- forming particularly well under scenarios involving dynamic class imbalance and concept drift. These findings highlight the potential of inference-time adaptation in challenging non-stationary environments and suggest that adaptation in memory- based stream classifiers need not rely exclusively on memory modification.

papers.title: Bandits with Probing: Optimal Coverage and the Role of Feedback
papers.summary: In bandits with probing, a learner selects at most $k$ of $n$ arms per round, earns the largest of their rewards, and competes with the best fixed single arm. For independent arms with i.i.d. rewards in $[0,1]$ and $2\le k<n$, the minimax regret is $Θ\bigl(\frac{n-k}{n}\min\{T,n/k\}\bigr)$, the cost of locating an unknown good arm, and observing only the maximum suffices to attain it. In particular, two probes give $Θ(\min\{T,n\})$ regret, which resolves two open questions of Bhaskara et al. (2023) with weaker feedback. Our policy turns the probing surplus, the excess of the maximum over each probed arm, into exploration capital, and a permanent random core yields the sharp dependence on $k$. On arbitrary fixed reward arrays, same-round contrasts between blocks of arms attain the same rate, because the surplus pays for the stability of mirror descent. Winner feedback, the maximum together with its winning label, instead incurs an additional learning cost under joint i.i.d. rewards and on fixed arrays. We characterize this cost even when values are revealed only intermittently, using policies that know neither the horizon nor the revelation rate. For three independent arms and two probes, exact maxima, Bernoulli-rounded maxima with winning labels, and winning labels alone have minimax regret $Θ(1)$, $Θ(\sqrt T)$, and $Θ(T)$: rounding preserves conditional means but not the rate.

papers.title: Principled Nonlinear Concept Erasure and Steering
papers.summary: Learned representations often encode sensitive attributes, such as gender or race, that may be undesirable or unsafe to retain. Concept erasure aims to remove this information while preserving task-relevant content. Existing methods remain incomplete: linear methods provide guarantees only against linear probes, while nonlinear methods achieve stronger empirical erasure but lack formal guarantees and often sacrifice utility. In this work, we introduce a principled conditional autoencoder framework for nonlinear concept erasure. We follow the principle that erasure should remove only the sensitive attribute and nothing else, and we show that, under the stated assumptions, perfect reconstruction together with population-level independence is sufficient for perfect nonlinear guardedness, with preservation guarantees in the imperfect-reconstruction regime. Empirically, we attain a superior utility-erasure trade-off across multiple datasets, sensitive attributes, and language models, surpassing even the supervised variants of competing methods despite using no target-task labels, while being simpler to optimize and converging substantially faster. Beyond erasure, our framework yields concept conversion (representation steering) as a by-product: by changing only the target concept at inference time, it produces representations corresponding to different concept values - at no additional training cost - a capability no prior erasure method provides, and on which we likewise demonstrate strong empirical performance.

papers.title: BAARC: Uncertainty-Driven Adaptive Partial Spectral Measurement to Full Reconstruction for Material Classification
papers.summary: Spectroscopic instruments with limited wavenumber coverage require accurate scan positioning or multiple measurements to complete the material analysis. This often requires prerequisite knowledge about the material under diagnosis to measure the spectral regions with distinguishing peaks. In our study, we simulate a Bayesian Adaptive Acquisition with Reconstruction-driven Classification (BAARC) framework for Raman spectral measurements, using masked training to learn spectral features that dynamically drive laser channel selection until the material is identified. We present a jointly trained two-level framework that takes progressive partial measurements of small wavenumber patches across the complete spectral range and, at each step, first attempts to reconstruct the full spectra until the model uncertainty is low. Secondly, material classification is performed at each reconstruction step until stoppage. Uncertainty quantification during reconstruction steps helps determine the measurement position of our next patch, while combining it with classification uncertainty determines measurement termination. By closing the loop between hardware acquisition and deep probabilistic modeling, the proposed system minimizes physical measurement steps while maintaining both spectral fidelity and diagnostic accuracy. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that our framework achieves high-accuracy sample identification using only a fraction of full-spectrum channels, offering a scalable solution for real-time, high-throughput spectroscopic instruments.

papers.title: DRIVE: Fine-tuning via Data Contribution- and Diversity-aware Weighting with Prior Regularization
papers.summary: Single-stage fine-tuning is pervasive, yet catastrophic forgetting persists when the source pre-training data is inaccessible. Data weighting affords a natural lever to modulate sample influence. Yet existing weighting methods lack a principled mechanism to explicitly arbitrate knowledge retention against new-task adaptation, and provide no unified differentiable objective to accommodate auxiliary signals such as sample diversity and sample characteristics. This is because current schemes privilege one goal over the other, and no explicit gradient-compatible encoding exists for such signals. To address this, we propose DRIVE, a principled and efficient weight assignment framework. It derives per-sample weights via a unified differentiable objective where three coupled signals co-evolve: Shapley additivity splits contribution into anti-forgetting and adaptation components, which are reshaped by a covariance-based diversity term and stabilized by a sample-characteristic prior. Far from a mere combination, this yields an end-to-end gradient-based scheme balancing stability against plasticity. Theoretically, we prove that DRIVE enjoys superior stability-plasticity guarantees over existing weighting schemes and enhances parameter estimation robustness. Empirically, it attains superior overall performance, faster convergence, and stronger robustness. Code at https://github.com/luciabcd/DRIVE.

papers.title: State Estimation as In-context Tabular Prediction
papers.summary: This letter poses state estimation (SE) as an in-context tabular prediction (ICTP) problem. The key idea is a tabular arrangement in which historical measurement vectors and corresponding state estimates serve as the context, and a new measurement vector forms the query for which we predict a state vector. We propose to use tabular foundation models (TFMs), pretrained on synthetic data, whose weights are never updated, so power system data is needed only as context. With frozen TFM weights we estimate the state of 14-, 30-, 33-, 70-, and 118-bus transmission and distribution networks, and do so where weighted least squares (WLS) fails or degrades, under low observability and with bad data. ICTP errors are 11 to 57$\times$ below the per-bus average of the context at full metering, and 1.3 to 4.0$\times$ below it with only 5% of measurements available. With measurements at six buses biased by 8$σ$, the ICTP angle error rises 1.8 to 5.0$\times$ over its bias-free value against 2.5 to 12.7$\times$ for WLS with bad-data detection. Without retraining, ICTP has lower voltage error than DSS$^2$ on both of its feeders, and lower than a retrained TAPINE on two of three reconfiguration sets.

papers.title: Foundations of the Scaling Law

Independent feature coverage gives $α_D=(β-1)/ζ$ from predictive-weight decay $β$ and occurrence rarity $ζ$. Separable-loss optimization determines training allocations and deployment crossovers. Nonlinear scoring can produce apparent emergent abilities, while grokking concerns delayed generalization and verification constrains test-time scaling. For regular molecular configurations, the $\mathrm{SE}(3)$ quotient gives $d_{\mathrm{int}}=d-6$ and relative approximation-exponent gain $6/d_{\mathrm{int}}$. Optimized dense-to-equivariant excess-loss ratios scale as $C^{p_{\mathrm{eq}}-p_{\mathrm{dense}}}$, where $p_j$ are compute-loss exponents and the prefactor depends on loss amplitudes and FLOP costs. papers.title: Sharpness-aware Orthogonalized Momentum Algorithms
papers.summary: Adversarial sharpness penalty per iteration of a base optimizer, known as sharpness-aware minimization (SAM), is an accepted technique to improve generalization in deep learning. Recently, Muon has emerged as a dominant optimization algorithm for training large language models (LLMs). It achieves lower sample complexity for heavy-tailed gradient updates - a phenomenon common in LLM training. However, sharpness penalties with Muon updates are yet largely unexplored in the literature. Moreover, the behavior of SAM under heavy-tailed noise is unknown both theoretically and empirically. A potential reason for this gap is the additional cost of extra gradient computation per iteration for penalty perturbations in SAM, which becomes prohibitive for LLMs. This paper introduces Sharpness-aware Orthogonalized Momentum Algorithm (SOMA) to combine a computationally efficient and theoretically grounded perturbation scheme with the Muon algorithm. The key idea is to use stale (purely) stochastic gradient noise for adversarial perturbations. Theoretically, we show that SOMA's sample complexity is invariant to the perturbation direction. We provide explorations and insights into SOMA's robustness to heavy-tailed gradient noise. We extensively explore SOMA's efficacy in (a) mitigating quality degradation due to post-training quantization, and (b) catastrophic forgetting during fine-tuning of LLMs.

papers.title: U-STS-LLM: A Unified Spatio-Temporal Steered Large Language Model for Traffic Prediction and Imputation
papers.summary: Accurate spatio-temporal cellular traffic analysis is fundamental to the reliable operation of modern mobile networks, as it underpins load forecasting for congestion avoidance and missing-data imputation for continuity despite transmission errors. papers.title: Quantum-aware Transformer model for state classification
papers.summary: Entanglement is a fundamental feature of quantum mechanics, playing a crucial role in quantum information processing. However, classifying entangled states, particularly in the mixed-state regime, remains a challenging problem, especially as system dimensions increase. In this work, we focus on bipartite quantum states and present a data-driven approach to entanglement classification using transformer-based neural networks. Our dataset consists of a diverse set of bipartite states, including pure separable states, Werner entangled states, general entangled states, and maximally entangled states. We pretrain the transformer in an unsupervised fashion by masking elements of vectorized Hermitian matrix representations of quantum states, allowing the model to learn structural properties of quantum density matrices. This approach enables the model to generalize entanglement characteristics across different classes of states. Once trained, our method achieves near-perfect classification accuracy, effectively distinguishing between separable and entangled states. Compared to previous Machine Learning, our method successfully adapts transformers for quantum state analysis, demonstrating their ability to systematically identify entanglement in bipartite systems. These results highlight the potential of modern machine learning techniques in automating entanglement detection and classification, bridging the gap between quantum information theory and artificial intelligence.

papers.title: PROVE: Probabilistic Visual Grounding via Patch-Level Evidence for Vision-Language Models
papers.summary: Visual grounding with vision-language models such as CLIP typically produces a single deterministic relevance map for an image-query pair, without indicating whether the localisation is reliable or whether the referent is present at all. We introduce \textbf{PROVE} (\textbf{Pro}babilistic \textbf{V}isual Grounding via Patch-Level \textbf{E}vidence), a post-hoc evidential adapter that maps frozen CLIP patch features to per-patch Beta distributions without modifying the backbone. PROVE casts grounding as per-patch membership: each patch accumulates positive and negative evidence for whether it belongs to the referent, so a query may match zero, one, or many patches. We train PROVE with an evidential objective on soft patch-coverage targets, and define a prior-pull objective that keeps absent-referent examples near an uninformative prior, so that vacuity serves as an absence signal without a dedicated presence classifier. During inference, a single forward pass yields, in closed form, a posterior-mean grounding map, a spatial vacuity map, and an image-level absence score. We evaluate PROVE on referring-expression benchmarks: it is competitive in localisation with state-of-the-art CLIP grounding methods, its uncertainty tracks localisation error and supports selective prediction under abstention, and its image-level score detects when the referent is absent altogether. Our evidential patch-membership modelling offers a simple, drop-in mechanism for probabilistic verification in frozen vision-language grounding systems.

papers.title: Data Quality Audit and Bivariate Temperature-Humidity Analysis of a Long-Term LoRaWAN Network: Anomaly Detection, PCA, Clustering and Machine Learning

papers.title: On the Limits of Stochastic Push-Pull over Time-Varying Digraphs
papers.summary: Stochastic Push-Pull achieves linear speedup with respect to the network size $n$ on static strongly connected digraphs, but whether this speedup persists on time-varying networks remains unclear. In this work, we construct a quadratic decentralized problem on period-two networks showing that stochastic Push-Pull may fail to attain linear speedup over time-varying digraphs. For $p$-periodic networks, we identify an effective node count $n_{\mathrm{eff}}\le n$ that governs the leading stochastic term. Specifically, for smooth nonconvex objectives, we establish convergence upper bounds and matching lower bounds for stochastic Push-Pull with constant stepsizes, both exhibiting the leading-order dependence $Θ(1/\sqrt{n_{\mathrm{eff}} T})$. When $p=1$, the identity $n_{\mathrm{eff}}=n$ recovers the usual linear speedup for static digraphs. However, periodic networks can have $n_{\mathrm{eff}}=o(n)$, demonstrating the loss of linear speedup under temporal variation. Numerical experiments illustrate effective-count scaling and the separation between static and periodic networks, consistent with our theoretical findings.

papers.title: Joint user-item allocation for e-commerce marketing campaigns
papers.summary: Web platforms run many marketing campaigns at once, and for each one they must decide which products to promote and which users to target. The best users depend on the products, and the best products on the users. The campaigns also compete with one another, because each user and each item may belong to only one of them and each audience is capped by the campaign budget. Still, existing approaches fix one side and search the other, choosing an assortment and then looking for its audience, or ranking items for one user at a time. Either way they solve a restricted version of the full problem, implying that a jointly optimized assignment would be at least as good and possibly far better. What the restriction costs, and whether the joint problem is solvable at the scale campaigns are run, remain unknown. Here we formalize the joint task as auto-targeting: assigning users and items to multiple disjoint, capacity-bounded campaigns that maximize the affinity between them. We adapt constrained spectral biclustering, greedy local search with pairwise swaps, and a multi-armed bandit formulation to the task and compare them against the conventional decoupled baseline. On synthetic data, two Amazon Reviews benchmarks, and two proprietary commercial datasets, auto-targeting raises campaign lift over the best decoupled pipeline, from around 20\% on the two smaller, denser datasets to more than threefold on the two largest. Biclustering yields the highest campaign quality across datasets, while bandit-based methods run fastest on the largest ones.

papers.title: When Does Dynamics Randomization Test Context Inference?
papers.summary: Environments with randomized dynamics are widely used to ask whether world models need explicit context inference. However, randomization can leave little predictive information for a context encoder to add, because distinct latent parameters may produce similar transitions at visited states, or those states may already reveal the active context. We formalize the remaining one-step information as predictive headroom and compare kernels under fixed and visited state--action distributions to distinguish changes in query coverage from changes in context weights. We analyze discrete and continuous environments and find low headroom both when kernels differ little and when visitation reduces an otherwise large discrepancy. At the same time, resetting state components increases headroom, showing that context evidence accumulates in state. We propose reporting this headroom alongside the randomized parameters, so that gains from explicit context inference can be interpreted relative to the information missing from the current state and action.

papers.title: Harmful Responses Are Jailbreak Templates: Transferring Autoregressive Jailbreaks to Diffusion Language Models
papers.summary: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) enable flexible masked generation through bidirectional context modeling, but this capability also introduces a distinct jailbreak attack surface. papers.title: A Measure-Geometric Theory of Robustness in Machine Learning
papers.summary: This paper develops a foundational measure-geometric theory of robustness in machine learning. Robustness is formulated as escape from a retained task state relative to a reference measure on a data-bearing manifold, a perturbation gauge, and an admissible realization mechanism. papers.title: Detection and Validation of Hidden Subgroup Disparities in Clinical AI
papers.summary: Machine learning (ML) models used in clinical workflows often perform systematically differently across patient groups, raising concerns about equity and patient safety. As a proof of concept, we also showed that annotations from learned subgroups can be used to mitigate the biases they expose. We conclude that subgroup discovery is a practical and effective tool to enhance the performance validation and monitoring of ML systems in healthcare.

papers.title: Instance-dependent Stochastic Lipschitz bandit
papers.summary: We study the Lipschitz bandit problem, where a learner sequentially maximizes an unknown Lipschitz function $f$ over a domain $\mathcal{X} \subset [0,1]^d$ using noisy pointwise evaluations. However, such zooming-based guarantees are only partially instance-dependent, as they depend solely on the asymptotic growth of near-optimal level sets and fail to capture finer structural properties of $f$. We provide an analysis and an algorithm that characterizes the regret through integrals of the suboptimality gap of $f$ over its level sets. This yields regret bounds that adapt to the local growth of level sets, rather than only their asymptotic behavior. As a corollary, when the set of maximizers has dimension $d^\star>0$, we obtain improved adaptive rates of order $\tilde{\mathcal{O}} \left ( T^{d_z+1 / \max(d_z,d^\star)+2}\right )$ strictly improving over classical zooming bounds in this regime. Finally, we extend our analysis to the full-information setting (Lipschitz experts) and show how some of the regularity assumptions can be relaxed.

papers.title: Feature-Space Smoothing: Certified Robustness of Deep Representations
papers.summary: Modern deep learning models exhibit strong capabilities across diverse applications, yet remain vulnerable to malicious inputs that induce erroneous predictions via feature-space distortion. Building on those insights, we introduce the Gaussian Smoothness Booster (GSB), a plug-and-play module to improve the encoder Gaussian robustness score. Specifically, the GSB module is plugged to enhance the feature-space consistency and maintain the feature utility for downstream tasks under Gaussian perturbations. This design enables seamless integration of FS on the protected model, e.g., Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), without additional model retraining or alignment, improving its robustness while preserving the performance for downstream task-oriented decoding. papers.title: Recurrent Self-Improvement: Dynamic Cross-Loop On-Policy Distillation for Looped Language Models
papers.summary: Looped Language Models (LoopLMs) offer a parameter efficient approach to scaling reasoning by reusing shared parameters across recurrent computation steps. We further propose Dynamic LoopOPD (D-LoopOPD), which continually refreshes the terminal loop teacher as the shared model parameters are updated, enabling recurrent self-improvement. We characterize how distillation updates propagate across loop depths and derive sufficient conditions under which a single update yields simultaneous local improvement at both loop depths. Experiments on Ouro-Thinking models show that LoopOPD improves mathematical reasoning, while D-LoopOPD yields further gains through dynamic teacher updates. Despite being trained only on mathematical data, the resulting models also improve on general reasoning and code generation benchmarks, demonstrating that recurrent computation can serve as an effective source of supervision for LoopLMs. Our code and model checkpoints will be released upon acceptance.

papers.title: Empirical concentration for chains with infinite memory

While some regularity assumptions are required to make the bounds empirical, our procedure remains fully adaptive in the sense that it does not require the knowledge of the constants involved in these assumptions. papers.title: $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{T})$ Regret and Polylogarithmic Constraint Violation for COCO
papers.summary: We study constrained online convex optimization with adversarial convex costs and constraints ($\mathsf{COCO}$). Consequently, the learner incurs a cost of $f_t(x_t)$ and a constraint violation of $\max\{0,g_t(x_t)\}$, and aims to simultaneously minimize regret and cumulative constraint violation ($\mathsf{CCV}$) over the entire horizon. The key observation is that whenever the mean of the Hedge distribution violates a constraint, Grünbaum's inequality guarantees that a constant fraction of the Hedge probability mass is eliminated. We use an adaptive learning-rate schedule and a potential function coupling the surviving volume with the learning rate to convert this probability-mass reduction into a bound of $O(\log^2 T)$ on the $\mathsf{CCV}$.

papers.title: Do Halting Heads Really Save Compute in Looped Language Models?
papers.summary: Looped language models run each token through the same layers several times, and each run is one iteration. To save compute, an extra layer, the halting head, gives after each iteration the probability that the token stops there, so that easy tokens can stop early. Pretraining models from scratch, up to 1.3B parameters, we find two problems. First, heads trained on a mix of all iterations predict that tokens need under half the iterations, yet under the standard stopping rule tokens run almost every iteration, because this training never scores the single iteration where a token stops. Scoring every iteration instead fixes this, but in our runs it works only with a strong penalty favoring early stops. Second, savings are commonly reported as an average number of iterations per token, but when sequences are generated in batches that run until their slowest token stops, a model without a head is almost as good at that cost. The reported average can therefore overstate the saving. We recommend reporting the iterations tokens actually run, with the stopping threshold and batch size, and give a test, run before training a head, that bounds its gain.

papers.title: Verdict Instability of OOD Scores under Reference Resampling

papers.title: Putting Transformer Theories to the Test
papers.summary: Several formal theories have been developed to characterize the capabilities and limitations of the transformer architecture, each employing different abstractions that capture different features of the architecture. Together, our results point to several specific features that a theory of transformers must capture: soft rather than hard attention, dynamic content-dependent retrieval, bounded computation at each position, an account of learnability and inductive biases, and a combination of upper and lower bounds.

papers.title: Agreement rather than normalisation keeps depth reusable in looped language models
papers.summary: Looped language models apply one block of layers repeatedly, and the design pays off only if depth is reusable: loop steps beyond the trained budget must remain usable at inference. We ask whether that rests on normalising the state between loop steps, as the released Ouro models do, or on agreement between the loop a model is trained with and the loop it is run with. On released weights this loop-boundary normalisation can be removed without adding parameters and with the readout path bit-identical, and the operation is an identity at one loop step, which serves as an implementation check. Removing it takes Ouro-1.4B and Ouro-2.6B to zero accuracy by the trained budget on a balanced binary task (chance 0.500). State-norm growth, the failure that prior accounts predict, is not the cause: the norm stays within a factor of 2.021 while the head commits to a single wrong token. Yet in 19M-parameter models trained from scratch on two synthetic tasks, 16 seeds per configuration, training without the normalisation is never worse than training with it and extrapolates better: the two are closest at the trained depth and separate on both sides of it (Cliff's delta up to 0.867 beyond the budget). Both results follow if agreement, and not the normalisation itself, is what keeps depth reusable. The damage sits in the readout together with the last layer of the block: in the models trained from scratch, refitting the head over the frozen modified loop recovers a third of the lost accuracy and plateaus, while refitting the last block layer with it recovers all of it. Finally, comparing looped with stacked depth at an equal inference loop count is confounded by unequal overshoot of the trained budget; at matched overshoot the advantage of looping vanishes on one task and shrinks on the other.

papers.title: Every Weight Is a Path of Shared Discrete Decisions
papers.summary: We introduce TWIG (Tree-structured Weights with Inherited Gates), a representation in which every weight of a neural network is the end of a path of small discrete decisions: a sign, a shift by a power of two, a zero gate, an index into a shared table. Weights that belong together share the upper part of their paths, and each decision is inherited by every weight below it, so it is stored once and applied once. This simple change has three consequences. Any trained network can be written as a TWIG, and when the decisions are powers of two its weight layers become circuits made almost entirely of wires and adders, suited to chips whose weights are fixed at fabrication. Pruning, quantization, low-rank factorization, codebooks and weight sharing become edits of one object, so a single optimizer can choose among all of them for a whole network. And choosing the decisions is the ground-state problem of a higher-order Boltzmann machine whose interactions follow the paths of the tree, the problem class that annealers and quantum optimizers are built to solve. Today these questions are handled apart: each compression method brings its own format and solver, a circuit with fixed weights needs a dedicated constant multiplier for every weight, and discrete solvers reach only narrow subproblems such as rounding. Weight formats have long been moving toward shared decisions, through group scales, shared exponents, microexponents and sparse weights; TWIG takes this trend to its end, and every common format is a shallow TWIG at no extra cost. On five weight matrices of a large language model, a flat tree whose signed power-of-two terms are chosen per weight for circuit cost, with no group scales, needs 9--15\% fewer additions than GPTQ at equal layer error at 3- and 4-bit accuracy on typical matrices, and 20--55\% fewer on matrices with strong outliers.

papers.title: Decode Late, Multiply Once: Rethinking the Dot Product for Quantized Weights
papers.summary: Large neural networks are increasingly deployed with 1-4 bit weights and 16- or 32-bit activations, yet their dot products still use one multiplier per element. We show that a length-n dot product with k-bit weight codes can be computed with n+2^k additions and at most 2^k decodes and 2^k multiplications. Each weight code is used directly as an address offset that selects one of 2^k accumulators; each activation is added into the selected accumulator; and the accumulated sums are decoded and multiplied only once, at the end, in a fused decode-and-multiply step. The decoded weight vector is never formed. The refactoring is exact for integer arithmetic, works with integer or floating-point operands and with arbitrary, including nonlinear, decoders, and extends to group-wise scales and to matrix and tensor products. The multiplier count falls by n/2^k, while total arithmetic energy improves by a smaller, bounded factor that we quantify with a cost model. We describe a scatter-accumulate processing element (SA-PE) that replaces the MAC unit in a weight-stationary systolic array, with a load/stream/reduce/drain schedule in which a small, time-shareable multiplier runs only 2^k times per tile. Because decoded weights are not stored, local weight memory shrinks by up to w_d/k for w_d-bit decoded weights. An RTL implementation synthesized for FPGA and compared with a matched MAC array shows that an unshared SA-PE is larger than a MAC PE, and that the saving appears when the reduction multiplier is shared across PEs. Software models confirm exact integer equivalence and floating-point error no worse than the conventional pipeline. We do not claim the underlying identity is new, and we discuss related work on weight sharing and lookup-based kernels.

papers.title: A Fix for Softmax and Cross-Entropy

papers.title: Under the Influence: Evaluating and Improving LLM Vigilance in Agentic Tasks
papers.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are becoming increasingly autonomous assistants, capable of accomplishing series of complex tasks by interacting with open world domains such as software databases and the internet. While well-studied in humans, the extent to which LLM agents exhibit vigilance is relatively unknown. Here, we examine LLM agent vigilance in three realistic tasks: navigating dangerous websites, avoiding e-commerce scams, and patching an unsafe code repository. We find that all frontier models are highly susceptible to malicious influence across all environments. We also find that model performance itself is surprisingly dissociable from vigilance. In light of these results, we propose a vigilance harness which uses Bayesian reasoning over a model's estimates of the value of an advisor's advice to decide whether to act on that advice. The vigilance harness helps recover baseline performance while retaining the benefit of positive influence on agents, paving the way for safer agentic AI systems.

papers.title: BeNice! Closing Looping's Inference-Memory Gap via KV-Sharing
papers.summary: Looped architectures scale quality while keeping parameter count fixed by repeatedly passing activations through the same block of layers. During inference, each recurrence generates independent KV-caches, causing memory to grow linearly. To address this challenge, prior work has proposed KV-sharing (i.e., sharing KV-caches across depth), finding that, in some cases, the KV-cache of the final recurrence can be shared with the earlier recurrences without quality loss, a property we denote as KV-shareability. However, the mechanisms underlying KV-shareability remain poorly understood, with even identically trained looped architectures not consistently exhibiting it. In this paper, we study how KV-shareability can be enabled in looped models. We propose a two-stage method: in the first stage, we use stochastic depth during pretraining, which induces contractive residual dynamics that drive representations toward a common limit across recurrences. In the second stage, we propose BeNice!, a post-training method that broadcasts the final recurrence's KV-cache into the first recurrence, training it to produce compatible residuals while preserving the original model's quality. As a result, BeNice! enables KV-shareability while matching standard finetuning's unshared validation perplexity. Using BeNice!, we show that KV-sharing is complementary to alternative KV-compression methods, composing with memory-efficient sequence mixers (e.g., multi-latent attention, Kimi delta attention) and low-precision KV-cache quantization (e.g., fp8, mxfp8, nvfp4). Finally, in simulated low-memory, long-context inference, KV-sharing improves cache hit rates by up to 31.4%, increases throughput by up to 23.6%, and reduces p90 time-to-first-token by up to 83.6%.

papers.title: OP-Print: Tracing Membership Imprints in On-Policy Self-Distillation
papers.summary: On-policy distillation has been widely adopted for alleviating the distribution mismatch of off-policy distillation. papers.title: Efficient and Optimal Learning of Discrete Distributions with Person-Level Privacy
papers.summary: We study learning a discrete distribution under person-level differential privacy in the batched setting. Under pure $(\varepsilon,0)$-DP, we achieve $n = \widetilde O(k/(α^2 m)+k/(α\sqrt{m}\varepsilon)+k/\varepsilon)$, the first polynomial-time pure-DP guarantee matching the information-theoretic optimum up to logarithmic factors. Under approximate $(\varepsilon,δ)$-DP, we achieve $n = \widetilde O(k/(α^2 m)+k/(α\sqrt{m}\varepsilon)+k+\log(1/δ)/\varepsilon)$. At $δ=2^{-Θ(k)}$, this is $\widetilde O(k)$ for fixed $α,\varepsilon,m$ and failure probability. Our algorithms use a new degree-6 sum-of-squares estimator for learning from untrusted batches. Its key ingredient is a trace-bounded diagonal majorizer for the difference between the empirical covariance of the repaired batch averages and the multinomial covariance predicted by their mean. We prove that clean data admit this certificate through semidefinite-programming duality and a new application of the stronger symmetric form of Grothendieck's inequality due to Friedland and Lim. The certificate preserves the mean-dependent variance of multinomial batch averages, yielding the near-optimal robust rate $O(η\sqrt{\log(1/η)/m})$ and providing the score required by the privacy reduction. papers.title: Action Learning for Scientific Simulations
papers.summary: Understanding and controlling how systems evolve is central to science and engineering, where many problems require reasoning about complete trajectories. Existing approaches typically learn local dynamics or generate trajectories, but objectives constructed from individual transitions can miss dependencies across time, while generative models do not necessarily provide a tractable objective for evaluating and optimizing arbitrary paths. This construction yields a differentiable objective on path space that can capture both local dynamical structure and nonadditive dependencies across time. We show that $\textit{action learning}$ is a promising framework for turning trajectory observations into reusable objectives for scientific inference and control.

papers.title: Rethinking Sequence Compression with Test-time Regression

papers.title: Fine-Grained Analysis of Catastrophic Forgetting in Continual Learning via Algorithmic Stability
papers.summary: Understanding catastrophic forgetting, in which learning new tasks degrades performance on previously learned tasks, remains a fundamental challenge in continual learning (CL). Specifically, we decompose forgetting into intra-task and cross-task generalization gaps and empirical forgetting. Finally, we conduct experiments on Split CIFAR-100 and Split MiniImageNet to examine the empirical implications of our theoretical findings.

papers.title: Robust Tangent Space Estimation via Laplacian Eigenvector Gradient Orthogonalization
papers.summary: Estimating the tangent spaces of a data manifold is a fundamental problem in geometric data analysis. papers.title: Multi-Token Prediction and Alternative Tokenization Improve Learning Latent Multi-Hop Graph Search at Scale
papers.summary: Given an unseen graph, a start node, $s$, and an end node, $t$, can a language model generate the shortest path from $s$ to $t$? Prior work has found that models fail to learn this task as the graphs scale. We show that this failure has two causes: the supervision signal and the tokenization. First, we theoretically establish and empirically demonstrate the effectiveness of multi-token prediction (MTP), and show that the benefits of MTP are topologically agnostic. Second, we introduce alternative tokenizations and show that the two causes are orthogonal. Using these methods, we break through the scaling wall observed by prior work, consistently and stably learning to solve the task at scales far beyond previous limits.

papers.title: Dimension-free regimes for unadjusted Langevin in ridge-separable models: A subspace robust Wasserstein analysis
papers.summary: The Unadjusted Langevin Algorithm (ULA) is widely used for high-dimensional Bayesian inference. Classical analyses in Wasserstein-2 distance predict an asymptotic bias and a mixing time that grow with dimension, but this metric is stronger than necessary for many statistical tasks. We instead analyze the bias in subspace robust Wasserstein distance, which controls the mean and arbitrary low-dimensional marginals and is therefore well suited to observables typically estimated in practice. For ridge-separable potentials formed with i.i.d. data, we prove high-probability bounds showing a bell-shaped mixing profile as the number of data points $N$ varies relative to the dimension $d$. In the overparameterized regime, the effective dimension is the rank $N$ of the data-dependent perturbation, leading to complexity depending on $N$ rather than $d$. In the large-sample regime, Gaussian-perturbation estimates yield dimension-free complexity once $N$ is sufficiently large. In contrast, near the proportional regime $\asymp d$, we prove that dimension-free guarantees are impossible in general.

papers.title: Residual Correlation as a Diagnostic for Joint-Uncertainty Gains from GP Coregionalisation
papers.summary: In multi-target regression, correlated targets are often coupled through multi-output Gaussian processes with an intrinsic model of coregionalisation (GP-ICM), assuming that sharing statistical strength improves overall performance. In practice, the benefits are inconsistent. Across the settings studied, we find that the main benefit of coregionalisation is joint uncertainty quantification rather than point prediction. Raw target correlation does not predict when coupling helps; in the separable GP-ICM settings studied here, residual correlation, the cross-target dependence left unexplained by independent per-target predictors, is the strongest predictor of joint-uncertainty gains. We introduce a lightweight diagnostic, $D_{\rm logdet}=-\frac{1}{2}\log\det R_{\rm res}$, which represents the idealised joint negative log-likelihood (NLL) gain from modelling a full rather than diagonal residual covariance and is computable from independent GPs alone. Across a controlled synthetic study, 16 multi-target benchmarks, and frozen transformer and convolutional neural network representations for keypoint regression, point prediction remains largely unchanged ($ΔR^2\approx 0$). In contrast, $D_{\rm logdet}$ strongly predicts observed ICM NLL improvements ($ρ_s=-0.83$, $p<0.001$), outperforming heuristics such as the feature-to-sample ratio. We also propose Residual-ICM, which preserves independent marginal variances while adding residual-correlation structure to the joint covariance. Residual-ICM achieves the best average joint NLL among the compared methods, while the diagnostic indicates when covariance coupling is likely to be useful. The diagnostic is specific to global Gaussian residual dependence, the structure captured by separable coregionalisation.

papers.title: When and How Does Muon Precondition? The Role of Structured Gradient Noise
papers.summary: Muon has become a popular optimizer for large language model training, yet its theoretical foundations remain poorly understood. In this work, we study how gradient noise geometry shapes Muon's preconditioning benefits. We first show, theoretically and empirically, that under the classical isotropic noise assumption, Muon offers no acceleration beyond a rescaling of the learning rate. This motivates us to investigate structured noise arising from mini-batch sampling in associative memory with heterogeneous task frequencies. We establish an exact balancing threshold for two tasks and extend the analysis to multiple tasks, revealing how task coverage and gradient reliability jointly shape learning. Our analysis shows that Muon can soften the dependence on task frequency from linear to square-root, helping balance the learning of frequent and rare tasks. We further identify rotation-induced negative transfer in SignSGD that Muon avoids, and explain how momentum reduces sampling noise while tracking changing gradients. Controlled numerical experiments validate these mechanisms, and a preliminary LLM pretraining study illustrates the practical promise of fast-slow momentum.

papers.title: SQuAT: Spherical Lattice Vector Quantization-Aware Training
authors: Tycho F. A. van der Ouderaa
papers.summary: Vector quantization (VQ), in particular lattice-based methods, offer strong rate-distortion trade-offs for low-bit large language models (LLMs), yet their behavior under quantization-aware training (VQ-QAT) remains poorly understood. We scale lattice VQ-QAT to billion-parameter LLMs and multi-billion-token training regimes, and introduce SQuAT, a shape-gain VQ-QAT approach trained with a separate straight-through estimator (STE) for the shape and gain. SQuAT decomposes weights into direction and magnitude: normalized directions are quantized using an $E_8$-derived spherical codebook, while gains are quantized independently with low-bit scalar quantizers. We show that, unlike a standard STE applied to the full quantizer, which ignores the shape-gain structure, these separate STEs induce tangent-space updates for directions, yielding an implicit form of spherical (Riemannian) optimization. To enable scalability, we develop a distributed exact nearest-neighbor assignment scheme, in which workers quantize disjoint weight blocks and communicate only discrete indices, reducing VQ-QAT training time by 12.8$\times$ and allowing us to scale it to 10B tokens. Across instruction-tuned LLaMA-3.2-1B/3B, Qwen3-4B, and base Qwen3-1.7B, SQuAT consistently outperforms standard VQ-QAT STE under identical quantizers and initialization, and achieves SOTA VQ-QAT accuracy.

papers.title: Deficit-Driven Stratified Acquisition for Building STRATA-S12: An Open SAR-Optical Corpus for Self-Supervised Learning
papers.summary: Building a co-registered SAR-optical corpus for self-supervised Earth Observation is above all an acquisition problem, yet the main multi-modal datasets are collected opportunistically, with no per-stratum quota control, so the regions and seasons that cloud cover hits hardest end up under-sampled. We present Deficit-Driven Stratified Acquisition (DDSA), an algorithm that casts the construction of a Sentinel-1/Sentinel-2 corpus as a constrained maximum-coverage problem over a land-cover-driven, hemisphere-corrected (class x season x region) stratification of target countries on all six inhabited continents, and solves it online: acquisition is ordered by marginal gain against a per-stratum deficit that the quality gates and a visual review of every accepted pair keep updating during the run. Three results follow from measuring the algorithm on its own product. First, stratum balance is a property of the deficit-driven ordering rather than of run length: replayed over all 2,928,370 real acquisition attempts, failures included, it populates all 192 strata within 0.05% of the attempts, against 4.03% for uniform round-robin effort and 20.5% for a random order. Second, whether a rejected attempt can be recovered is better predicted by how long its cause persists than by the type of defect: cloud rejections are recovered at eta = 18.8% against 41.4% for nodata, consistent with clouds persisting through a season. Third, the repair loop supplies 39.5% of the released pairs at no measurable quality cost, with 89.8% surviving manual review, but it adds yield rather than balance. The quality guarantee has a price: 2,928,370 acquisition attempts produced 740,746 released pairs. We release the corpus, STRATA-S12, with per-pair metadata sidecars aligned with the STAC and PDS4 standards and the FAIR principles, and a pre-registered linear probe confirms it is fit for self-supervised pre-training.

papers.title: Giskard : Byzantine Robust and Private Aggregation for Large-Scale Decentralized Learning
papers.summary: In decentralized learning, clients train a machine learning model while keeping their data locally and share their model parameters or gradients with a set of neighbors, making it vulnerable to both privacy attacks and model poisoning attacks. Jointly addressing privacy and Byzantine behavior in decentralized learning is challenging. Indeed, Differential Privacy (DP) applied on the client side is known to increase the variance of honest model updates, which weakens Byzantine-robust aggregation against poisoning attacks. Distributed DP can mitigate this issue by adding noise after aggregation, but implementing it without a trusted curator requires both confidential and Byzantine-resilient computation. Recent work addresses this challenge using secure multi-party computation (MPC) to implement robust aggregation while preserving input confidentiality. However, these solutions scale badly: they either require all-to-all communication between participants or delegate the entire computation to a small subset of parties whose computational and communication cost grows with network size. In this paper, we present Giskard, a scalable protocol for private and Byzantine-robust decentralized aggregation. Giskard organizes $n$ parties into a tree of committees of size $O(\log n)$ and evaluates a differentially private coordinate-wise approximate median via a committee-adapted secure quantile search over the value domain, using MPC within each committee. We assess Giskard both theoretically by proving its security and privacy properties and empirically through extensive experiments involving up to one million participants. Compared to its closest competitors, Giskard reduces per-party communication complexity by close to three orders of magnitude over the closest competitor while exhibiting comparable robustness under up to $n/4$ Byzantine parties.

papers.title: AfterDeleteBench: Auditing Post-Deletion Information Persistence in LLM Agents
papers.summary: Many LLM agents maintain external persistent memory and derive additional state from past interactions, such as summaries. Deleting an original memory record therefore need not remove information carried by its descendants. We introduce AfterDeleteBench, a controlled behavioral audit for this failure mode in fixed-weight LLM agents. For each synthetic secret, we compare an exposed-then-deleted agent with an otherwise matched agent that was never exposed to the secret, allowing post-deletion recovery to be attributed to the original exposure. In our primary setting, a single query recovers the deleted secret from Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct in roughly two thirds of cases, while matched never-exposed controls have zero recovery. Crucially, recovery does not require a surviving verbatim copy: when the complete secret string is absent and only separately stored components remain under a public composition rule, exact reconstruction succeeds in 62-99% of cases across Qwen, Mistral, and Phi-3. We also show that the response interface is part of the measurement system: target-bearing replies can be scored as failures when the requested format and parser are misaligned. Finally, we separate reconstruction from write-back and fresh-session recall. Provenance-aware closure eliminates observed recovery in the tested positive-baseline settings, whereas an exact-literal write filter blocks reinsertion but cannot erase information already present. Together, these results show that source deletion should be evaluated behaviorally at the level of the agent and its memory system, not only as a storage operation.

papers.title: Are EEG Sequences Time Series? EEG Classification with Time Series Models and Joint Subject Training
papers.summary: As with most other data domains, EEG data analysis relies on rich domain-specific preprocessing. Beyond such preprocessing, machine learners would hope to deal with such data as with any other time series data. For EEG classification many models have been developed with layer types and architectures we typically do not see in time series classification. Furthermore, typically separate models for each individual subject are learned, not one model for all of them. In this paper, we systematically study the differences between EEG classification models and generic time series classification models. We describe three different model setups to deal with EEG data from different subjects, subject-specific models (most EEG literature), subject-agnostic models and subject-conditional models. In experiments on three datasets, we demonstrate that off-the-shelf time series classification models trained per subject perform close to EEG classification models, but that do not quite reach the performance of domain-specific modeling. Additionally, we combine time-series models with subject embeddings to train one joint subject-conditional classifier on all subjects. The resulting models are competitive with dedicated EEG models in 2 out of 3 datasets, even outperforming all EEG methods on one of them.

papers.title: Can Entry-Wise Clipping Give Spectral Control of Stochastic Gradients?
papers.summary: Training instabilities such as loss spikes are frequently the result of stochastic gradient noise. Because of rare expressions in language training data, and multiple layer composition, the noise impact is heavy-tailed and survives mini-batch averaging. Existing remedies trade off structure against cost: vector-norm clipping ignores the matrix structure of weight updates, while spectral normalization (e.g., Muon (Jordan et al., 2024)) respects it at additional cost. We show that this trade-off can be balanced. Real gradient noise appears to be similar to entry-wise heavy-tailed contamination, and a first-order perturbation analysis reveals a localization property of such noise, under which a simple entry-wise method achieves spectral control. Exploiting this, we derive a tractable surrogate for the Bayes-optimal entry-wise estimator under a Gaussian signal prior. We establish $O(\varepsilon^{-4})$ convergence guarantee under Cauchy-contaminated noise. Empirically, we find that smooth shrinkage improves Adam on NanoGPT pretraining, saving ${\sim}7\%$ of training tokens. We further find that applying the entry-wise clipping before spectral normalization yields a ${\sim}2\%$ token saving on top of Muon.

papers.title: Disclosure Begets Disclosure: A Self-Reinforcing Privacy Loop in LLM Agents with Persistent Memory
papers.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly use persistent memory to personalize responses, and personal attributes in this memory pose a privacy risk if exposed. We ask how consulting memory during dialogue changes what users go on to say, and thus what the memory comes to reveal. In multi-session simulations, a simulated user with 24 personal attributes talks with a support agent that does or does not consult memory, and in both settings attributes are inferred from the full accumulated record. Across four support models, memory raises response quality but also empirical leakage, the share of attribute values correctly inferred from the record, by a margin that widens over sessions. The cause is a loop in ordinary, non-adversarial assistance. Memory-conditioned responses carry earlier values forward, often as presuppositions, and users affirm them or leave them uncorrected, so that cues and the agent's own guesses become recorded values. The loop reinforces itself, and removing the agent's mentions of an attribute lowers its later disclosure about twice as much as single-turn effects predict. Users cannot leave it on their own, since correcting a value discloses the attribute, declining to discuss it shifts later predictions toward sensitive values, and incorrect values left in place become entrenched. The loop is best weakened at the agent's response. Instructing the agent not to state or presuppose attributes brings leakage to about the no-memory level while keeping most of the quality gains, whereas filtering or anonymizing what users say or what is stored gives up much of them.

papers.title: Graph-Recurrent Learning of Emergent Collective Dynamics
papers.summary: Collective ordering in correlated electron systems emerges from microscopic dynamics, yet the evolution of observable textures need not admit a closed, memoryless description. We introduce a graph-recurrent neural network (GRNN) framework that learns such emergent dynamics directly from trajectories without specifying microscopic equations of motion. The framework integrates gated recurrent memory with graph message passing: local hidden states encode information beyond the instantaneous observables, while spatial coupling allows this information to propagate between sites. The observable and hidden fields evolve jointly through a shared local rule, providing a scalable representation of dynamics with spatial interactions and temporal memory. We demonstrate this framework on the emergent dynamics of charge-density-wave order in the semiclassical Holstein model, successfully reproducing temporal and spatial correlations and dynamical scaling during domain coarsening. By learning finite-time evolution directly, the GRNN offers a route to efficient, data-driven descriptions of collective dynamics with unresolved microscopic degrees of freedom.

papers.title: Show Me What You Don't Know: Efficient Sampling from Invariant Sets for Model Validation
papers.summary: The performance of machine learning models depends on discovering features in the data that are relevant to solving the given task while ignoring irrelevant variation. To check and visualize whether this is the case, we propose 'invariance auditing', a diagnostic tool to analyze feature extractors. Invariance auditing generates diverse inputs which all yield the same features as a given query input, and are therefore treated as identical by the model. Using external knowledge about the task at hand, this enables assessing if the learned invariances do or do not conform to the task's required semantics. Unlike existing work where a dedicated generative model is trained for each feature extractor, our algorithm is training-free and exploits a pretrained diffusion or flow-matching model to sample invariant inputs. Our fiber loss -- which penalizes feature mismatch -- guides the denoising process so the output shares the same representation as the query input. This replaces days of training with a single guided generation procedure at comparable quality. Experiments on popular datasets and model types demonstrate that our auditing method reveals invariances spanning very desirable and concerning behavior. For instance, it detects cases where Qwen-2B places patients with situs inversus (heart on the right side) in the same fiber as typical anatomy. Our code is available at https://github.com/vislearn/InvarianceAuditing.

papers.title: Fragility-aware Classification for Risk Characterization and Robust Learning
papers.summary: Classification models play a central role in data-driven decision-making applications such as medical diagnosis, recommendation systems, and risk assessment. Traditional performance metrics, such as accuracy and AUC, quantify classification errors and pairwise ranking performance but do not account for the magnitude of errors, i.e., the risk of confident misjudgments. This limitation is particularly consequential in safety-critical and cost-sensitive settings, where overconfident errors can lead to severe outcomes. To address this issue, we propose the Fragility Index (FI), a novel performance metric that evaluates classifiers from a risk-averse perspective by capturing the tail risk of confident misjudgments. We formulate FI within a robust satisficing (RS) framework to quantify classifier sensitivity under distributional uncertainty. Building on this, we develop a tractable surrogate-based training framework and establish provable bounds connecting training fragility to ranking-error FI. We further derive tractable reformulations for a broad class of loss functions, including cross-entropy, hinge-type, and Lipschitz losses, and identify specific conditions under which these reformulations are exact. We also introduce an FI-induced regularizer for deep neural networks. Empirical results on real-world medical diagnosis tasks demonstrate that FI complements existing metrics by revealing error tail risk not reflected in accuracy or AUC. FI-based models achieve competitive predictive performance while generally attaining lower FI. In the simulated human--AI diagnostic workflow, they also achieve lower average operational costs than empirical risk minimization.

papers.title: Deep Learning for Random Objects in Metric Spaces: Beyond Manifold Assumptions
papers.summary: Deep learning (DL) methods have substantially improved predictive performance across a wide range of downstream prediction tasks, enabling new discoveries in multiple domains. However, principled DL methods for non-Euclidean random objects remain relatively scarce, despite the growing importance of modern biomedical outcomes taking the form of probability distributions, random graphs, functions, and other random objects in metric spaces. Motivated by a new generation of digital and clinical biomarkers, we propose a deep learning framework for regression with random objects in metric spaces. Our approach operates directly on the metric structure of the response space, avoiding restrictive manifold or Euclidean embedding assumptions imposed by many existing methods. At the same time, it retains modern statistical guarantees under the stated statistical assumptions. We establish statistical consistency and convergence rates for the proposed estimator, and characterize conditions under which it can mitigate the curse of dimensionality for hierarchically compositional regression functions. Extensive simulation studies demonstrate competitive predictive performance, with gains over several competing approaches in multiple Euclidean and non-Euclidean configurations. Finally, we demonstrate the practical utility of the proposed framework in two digital health case studies with distribution-valued outcomes in Wasserstein spaces, using high-resolution accelerometry and continuous glucose monitoring data. Embedding-based deep-learning methods may be less suitable when no informative low-dimensional representation exists or when the learned embedding does not adequately preserve the intrinsic geometry of the response space.

papers.title: Identifiability from Stationary Covariance in Linear SDEs with Reciprocal Interactions and Latent Variables
papers.summary: Continuous-time stochastic differential equations (SDEs) provide a natural framework for modeling interacting dynamical systems. A central causal question is whether causal effects among observed variables can be identified from observational data drawn from the stationary distribution, given the underlying causal graph. papers.title: Extreme Compression of Per-Layer Embeddings via Cross-Layer Latent Vector Quantization
papers.summary: Scaling embedding capacity alongside Transformer computation is an emerging trend in language models. This trend makes high compression rates increasingly useful. Hence, we study extreme compression of Per-Layer Embeddings (PLE), which follow this trend and account for 35.2% of the parameters of Gemma 4 E4B. papers.title: The Bayesian Learning Rule Beyond KL Geometry
papers.summary: The Bayesian learning rule (BLR) exploits the relation between Bayesian updating and the Kullback-Leibler divergence (KLD) to derive efficient additive updates for exponential family variational posteriors. The KL geometry is powerful but restrictive: combined with posterior families with parameter-dependent support it can lead to undefined objectives. We ask which non-KL geometries preserve the additive BLR computation. Previous works that use $f$-divergences suggest that this is only possible with the KLD. Here, we show that this is not true. We show that additive information-geometric optimization algorithms can be derived for the class of mixed-space Bregman or Fenchel-Young discrepancies. These discrepancies induce generalized maximum-entropy families, dual coordinates, and generalized-BLR canonical gradient updates, recovering the classical BLR. The generalized BLR leads to new algorithms that \textit{cannot} be derived from the KL-based BLR. For the Tsallis negentropy with quadratic statistics, the generalized BLR yields bounded-support and heavy-tailed $q$-Gaussian posteriors and an easy Newton-like implementation. Experiments up to CIFAR-100 illustrate controllable support and tail behavior and competitive performance.

papers.title: The Fenchel-Young Generalization of Bayesian Principles
papers.summary: Conjugate Bayes plays a key role in machine learning, ensuring computationally simple posterior updates. We generalize the variational principle behind this computation by using the Fenchel-Young (FY) inequality, which lets us define a generalized evidence lower bound beyond the KL geometry, and at equality, characterizes new generalized posteriors. A generalized notion of conjugacy follows, defined as closure of prior-potential families that are affine under translation by the loss. We show that such families not only preserve additive canonical updating, but also posterior inference with parameter-dependent supports and tuneably heavy tails. This combination is not feasible with standard conjugate Bayes. We derive a new FY generalization of expectation maximization (EM), which recovers classical and Hard EM, and amortized versions. We show examples, including generalized Bayesian linear regression with closed-form bounded support and heavy-tailed posteriors, and a Gaussian mixture with sparse cluster assignments.
